pool.prompt: A splicer arrives to begin work but finds no records identifying which cable entries should connect to which. Who is primarily responsible for this gap?
choices: The splicer — they should have requested the records before arriving
The designer — the splice map (which fibers/buffer tubes connect at each case) is part of the design package handed to the splicer
The test technician — they own all documentation
No one — splice records are created entirely by the splicer during splicing
pool.explanation: The designer produces the splice design (splice map) as part of the design package — which fibers connect to which, which buffer tubes are through-spliced vs. broken out. The splicer creates individual fiber splice records (actual loss, fiber-by-fiber detail) during work, but the splice map itself comes from design. Arriving without it is a design-to-field handoff failure.

pool.prompt: An inspector finds a span where fiber cable hangs below the minimum ground clearance required by permit. What is the inspector's correct next action?
choices: Add it to the punch list and notify the PM — the construction crew must correct it before acceptance
Immediately call the electric utility to report a hazard
Adjust the cable sag themselves using tools in their truck
Accept the span since small clearance violations are typically waived
pool.explanation: The inspector's job is to identify and document non-conformances, not to fix them. Punch-listing the violation and notifying the PM triggers the correct correction workflow — the construction crew adjusts the installation, and the inspector re-inspects. Inspectors performing construction corrections themselves would compromise their independence as a QA function.

pool.prompt: What is the role of the licensed engineer who stamps and signs OSP construction drawings on an RUS-funded project?
choices: PE (Professional Engineer) — certifies the drawings meet applicable codes and are structurally sound, and is personally liable for that certification
PM (Project Manager) — coordinates schedule and budget but has no stamping authority
Staker — collects field survey data but does not review or certify designs
Test technician — verifies fiber performance, not drawing accuracy
pool.explanation: The PE (Professional Engineer) is state-licensed to certify engineering work. Their stamp is a legal certification they personally stand behind, carrying professional liability — a PE who stamps inaccurate work risks license suspension or revocation. RUS-program work requires PE-stamped drawings.
pool.citation: State professional engineering licensing requirements (NCEES-administered PE licensure is standard across US states).

pool.prompt: Who performs the final acceptance testing of a completed fiber plant, generating the formal Tier 1 and Tier 2 test records?
choices: The splicer — the in-process OTDR checks made during splicing are the same as the acceptance test
The make-ready crew — they perform final verification before the permit is closed
The test technician — performing bidirectional OTDR traces and end-to-end insertion loss tests on every fiber against the design's acceptance criteria
The designer — they set the acceptance criteria and personally verify the plant against them
pool.explanation: The test technician performs the formal, independent, end-to-end acceptance test on every fiber in the as-built plant. The splicer's per-splice OTDR checks are real-time quality checks during splicing, not the acceptance test.

pool.prompt: What does a make-ready crew do, and who do they typically work for?
choices: They install the new fiber cable; they work for the fiber company
They move, raise, or rearrange EXISTING attachments on shared poles to restore NESC clearances for the new attachment; they work for the pole owner (or an authorized contractor)
They perform final acceptance testing; they work for the client's engineer
They stamp construction drawings; they work for the state licensing board
pool.explanation: The make-ready crew works for the pole owner (or its authorized contractor). They modify existing attachments to make room for the new fiber and restore required clearances — they do not install the new fiber themselves; that's the construction crew's job.

pool.prompt: On a small regional OSP contractor, one technician often performs multiple roles (e.g., staking AND permitting AND final OTDR testing). What is the risk this creates, according to standard field practice?
choices: There is no risk — combining roles is always safer because fewer people are involved

It's not inherently wrong, but documentation and final test records are exactly the tasks most likely to get skipped when one person is overloaded — and that gap surfaces years later during troubleshooting
Combining roles is illegal on any RUS-funded project
Combining roles eliminates the need for a PE stamp
pool.explanation: Small-shop OSP work often has one person wearing multiple hats — that's a normal reality, not a violation. The risk is that documentation and final test records are the tasks most likely to be shortcut under time pressure, and that gap becomes a costly problem for whoever troubleshoots the network years later.

pool.prompt: A test technician needs to determine pass/fail for a fiber's acceptance test. What must they have to make that determination?
choices: The make-ready completion notice
The design's loss budget / acceptance criteria to compare the measured OTDR and OLTS results against
The staker's field notes from the original route survey
The permitting specialist's list of executed permits
pool.explanation: A test technician without the design loss budget can measure loss but cannot determine pass/fail — pass/fail is always a comparison against the design's stated acceptance criteria for that specific fiber path.

pool.prompt: Match each OSP field role to what it delivers, and to whom.

items.label: Design package -> PM, Permitting team, Make-ready application team
Splice records + initial OTDR traces -> Test technician

pool.explanation: Each role has a defined handoff: the staker's field data feeds the designer; the design package feeds the PM, permitting, and make-ready teams; the splicer's records feed the test technician; the inspector's punch list feeds the PM for acceptance sign-off.
